extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing screenwriters, dramatists, and storytellers for film/television
extracted.subtask_description: Practical principles for designing and evaluating screen stories: choosing events, composing structure, and shaping scenes, beats, values, and sequences so that a film (or dramatic work) creates meaningful emotional impact. Focused on screenwriting but applicable to other storytelling media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of Story over Dialogue/Description
rubrics_metrics.description: The workplace sign reads 'Story Department' — story is primary; a good story makes a good film possible, while failure to make the story work virtually guarantees disaster.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate work first for story: if the underlying story fails, vivid images or clever dialogue cannot save it. A writer who cannot 'tell story' negates literary flourishes. Aim to make story the organizing principle of the screenplay before attending to dialogue or description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common Story Problems to Eliminate
rubrics_metrics.description: Root causes of bland or boring texts include lack of progression, false motivation, redundant characters, empty subtext, holes, and similar story problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When critiquing or revising, look for these pathologies explicitly. Ask whether motivations are real, whether characters are necessary, whether subtext exists, whether narrative progression occurs, and whether logical/causal holes remain. Fixing these is central to making a story work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core Questions of Story Design (Who, Want, Why, How, Obstacles, Consequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Designing story consists largely of answering: Who are these characters? What do they want? Why do they want it? How do they try to get it? What stops them? What are the consequences?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these six questions as the backbone of planning and evaluation. Each main character should have clear answers; scenes and events should relate to and reveal these answers. If any of these are fuzzy, the story will lack clarity and drive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of Craft to Enable Storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Craft is the sum total of techniques used to draw the audience into deep involvement, hold that involvement, and reward it with a moving and meaningful experience; mastery of craft frees the subconscious and enables revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat craft as learnable and essential: write, step back, analyze (Is it good? Does it work? Why not?), and rewrite. Use craft-conscious analysis to unblock the creative process and to move from impulse to deliberate composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disposition and Loves of the Storyteller
rubrics_metrics.description: A storyteller must possess certain loves/passions: love of story, the dramatic, truth, humanity, sensation, dreaming, humor, language, duality, perfection, uniqueness, beauty, and a secure love of self (confidence in calling oneself a writer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These dispositions are not mechanical rules but essential attitudes that fuel choice of material, depth of empathy, and commitment to revision. Cultivate these loves as part of professional formation; they inform aesthetic and moral choices in story design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story as Metaphor for Life — Avoid Portraiture and Spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Story must be an abstraction of life that discovers essences (Big-T Truth), not mere reportage of fact ('portraiture') nor an overstructured spectacle that substitutes kinetic thrills and effects for meaningful human truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a piece merely catalogs occurrences or relies on spectacle/CGI as an end in itself. A strong story abstracts life to reveal underlying truths and keeps technical/aesthetic elements subordinate to the living content of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance Sensory Perception and Imaginative Power
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong storytelling strikes a balance between sensory power (acute, vivid description) and imaginative power (creating what could be). Either extreme — pure reportage or pure fantasy — weakens story; harmony across the spectrum is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether writing overindexes on descriptive detail without structural/ideational thrust, or vice versa. Cultivate and combine both capacities when crafting scenes and selecting events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction Between Literary Talent and Story Talent
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary talent (beautiful use of language) is common; story talent (the capacity to convert life into meaningful story form) is rare and primary for film. Literary gifts are valuable but secondary to story talent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating scripts, prioritize the presence of story talent (ability to shape life into compelling events) over merely elegant prose. Use literary skill to serve story, not substitute for it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure: Composition of Events to Arouse Emotions and Express a View
rubrics_metrics.description: STRUCTURE is a selection of events from characters' life stories that is composed into a strategic sequence to arouse specific emotions and to express a specific view of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design structure by deliberate selection and ordering of events. Ask what to include/exclude and why—every event must serve the purpose of arousing emotion and expressing the intended thematic viewpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a Story Event
rubrics_metrics.description: A STORY EVENT creates meaningful change in the life situation of a character that is expressed and experienced in terms of a VALUE and is ACHIEVED THROUGH CONFLICT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge candidate events by three tests: (1) Does it create meaningful change for a character? (2) Is the change expressed in terms of value (e.g., love/hate, life/death)? (3) Is it motivated/achieved through conflict (not mere coincidence)? If not, it's not a true story event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story Values (value-charged conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: STORY VALUES are universal qualities of human experience that may shift from positive to negative or vice versa (alive/dead, love/hate, freedom/slavery, hope/despair, etc.). Values are the soul of storytelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing scenes and events, identify the value at stake and its charge at scene start and end. Values must be clear and perceptible; dramatic tension arises from changes in value through conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene as the Story Event — Every Scene Must Turn
rubrics_metrics.description: A SCENE is an action through conflict in more or less continuous time and space that turns the value-charged condition of a character’s life on at least one value with a degree of perceptible significance. No scene that doesn’t turn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine each scene: note the value's charge at the beginning and at the close. If the value remains unchanged, the scene is likely a nonevent (often mere exposition) and should be cut or reworked so it effects a value turn. Aim to 'round' scenes so each contains a turning point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat: Smallest Element of Structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A BEAT is an exchange of behavior in action/reaction. Beat by beat these changing behaviors shape the turning of a scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break scenes into beats (distinct behavior exchanges) and ensure each beat advances action/reaction toward the scene’s turning point. Use beats to build credibility and emotional escalation within the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence: Series of Scenes Culminating in a Determinant Change
rubrics_metrics.description: A SEQUENCE is a series of scenes—generally two to five—that culminates with greater impact than any previous scene; the capping scene delivers a more powerful, determinant change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize scenes into sequences with escalating stakes leading to a capping scene. Typical sequences are 2–5 scenes; plan pacing and escalation so each sequence resolves into a significant consequential change for the protagonist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene Unity Test (Could It Be Written 'In One'?)
rubrics_metrics.description: The test of whether a series of activities constitutes a true scene: could it have been written 'in one,' in a unity of time and place? If so, it is a single Story Event/scene, even if the writer chooses to cut through locations for cinematic reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 'in one' test to determine whether disparate camera setups are actually one scene or multiple scenes. This helps maintain clarity about where true value turns occur and prevents padding with activity that doesn’t change values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose-Driven Selection of Events
rubrics_metrics.description: From the vast flux of life story the writer must make choices. To answer 'What to include? To exclude? To put before and after what?' you must know your purpose: events must be composed to serve the purpose of arousing emotion and expressing idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before adding an event, ask what purpose it serves in the overall design. If it fails to advance emotion, theme, or character consequence, exclude or rework it. Purpose-driven selection prevents understructure and aimlessness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Exposition as Sole Justification for a Scene
rubrics_metrics.description: If a scene's sole justification is exposition (conveying information), a disciplined writer will trash it and weave its information into the film elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When exposition is necessary, embed it within scenes that also effect a value turn or reveal character through action. Prefer scenes that do work (change values) over scenes that only inform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict over Coincidence; Motivation over Chance
rubrics_metrics.description: A story cannot be built of accidental events alone—meaningful Story Events must be achieved through conflict rather than mere coincidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating plot developments, check if key changes are motivated by characters' conflicts and choices. Avoid relying on coincidences to produce turning points; motivate reversals through established character dynamics and obstacles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetics and Effects Serve Story (Means, Not Ends)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstractions (graphic design, visual effects, CGI, editing, color, sound) have no meaning in themselves; they are means to express the living content of story but must never become an end in themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess technical/aesthetic choices by whether they enrich and vanish behind the story (as in FORREST GUMP, MEN IN BLACK) rather than call attention to themselves. Use effects to serve character and value, not to substitute for narrative depth.
